title: Gen Z's digital literacy has fallen behind millennials' despite universal school laptops
dek: Introduce a tool before mastering the underlying skill and you guarantee the skill won't be learned—precisely what happened when 88% of American students received school laptops.
why: This episode demonstrates the principle 'tools before skill' through calculators, AI, SAT reform and international data, giving parents and teachers a working framework for deciding when to introduce technology.
who: Parents of K-12 and college students weighing whether to give children devices or teach AI, plus classroom teachers and education policymakers.
skip: The guest's opening personal anecdotes (3:14-4:15) carry minimal insight and can be skipped.

points.h: Teaching the skill must come before introducing the tool
points.body: This principle emerged from the 1980s calculator debate: when should children use calculators? Answer: 'when you no longer need one'—once students understand arithmetic, a calculator is an aid; introduce it before they do and it permanently blocks skill formation. Children learn only to operate the machine until someone approves. This is what's happening at scale in schools distributing laptops today.

points.h: Teachers mid-career confuse engagement with learning
points.body: Those most confident in technology aren't veteran educators (20+ years, who've seen before-and-after and mostly reject it) or newcomers (who prioritize relationship-building). They're mid-career teachers—5 to 15 years in—trained by technology themselves. They judge tech 'effective' because students stay engaged. But engagement and learning are different metrics: swiping TikTok keeps you engaged without teaching you anything.

points.h: Learning happens through biological synchrony between teacher and student
points.body: Horvath redefines empathy not as emotion or personality but as a 'transpersonal emergent property': when two people synchronise, their heart rates and breathing align, their brain images converge. In sync with a teacher, students don't listen passively—they think alongside the teacher. Comprehension and motivation spike. Screens have no biology; they can never synchronise and actively sever the empathy already flowing between people.

points.h: Technology amplifies rather than closes the equity gap
points.body: Neil Postman's 1995 air-conditioning metaphor holds: tools never bridge equity gaps; they enlarge them. Horvath ran a counterfactual on New York data—assume minority students use tech all day and white students never use it—and the equity gap didn't shrink; it expanded 26%. The variable that works is 'every student has a teacher who genuinely cares.' Tech can't solve that.

points.h: Growing up with tools actually undermines digital literacy
points.body: Horvath often asks at AI education forums: 'How old are you and who taught you to use AI?' The answer is typically 30-something—a generation that never took a class on it yet outperforms kids who grew up onscreen. Tests show Gen Z and Alpha score high only on 'operating tools,' falling behind across every dimension that defines real literacy: creative use, critical use, safe communication. Those abilities depend on knowledge you bring to the tool, not what the tool teaches.

points.h: When SAT embedded powerful calculators, students learned to trick them
points.body: Until 2013, only four of America's top 50 universities allowed calculators at the college level—schools insisted students master arithmetic first. Last year, SAT eliminated its no-calculator math section entirely, embedding a calculator so powerful it can 'crack' every problem. Now tutoring doesn't teach math; it teaches kids how to coax the machine into solving it for them.

points.h: Test scores rose because the tests themselves were quietly redefined
points.body: NAEP and tests that maintain their measures show reading at historic lows, math barely back to 1992 levels. Even working memory—'remember seven digits'—supposedly a fixed constant, has fallen from seven to 5.5. But SAT scores rose after last year's redesign because reading was redefined as skimming 75-word excerpts (one question per 54 words) and writing redefined as spotting spelling errors. Rename the test and scores improve.

points.h: Countries that rejected EdTech longest are now seeing the steepest declines
points.body: China, Japan, South Korea and Singapore were the globe's lightest users of education technology before COVID—despite digital-dependent economies, they'd never scaled tech into classrooms. The pandemic forced adoption. Since then, even Singapore, whose test scores only ever climbed, has seen performance fall noticeably.

terms.def: Empathy redefined as biological synchrony between two people—their heart rates, breathing and brain activity align—rather than as individual personality or emotion.
The National Assessment of Educational Progress, a U.S. standardized test that uses the same scale every two years since 1992 to track American student achievement.
Formative assessment allows repeated feedback and revision; summative assessment is a one-time score with no opportunity to improve.
A digital literacy assessment measuring across four dimensions: tool operation, creative use, critical use and safe communication.

quotes.text: So when brought in after you've developed the skill, it's just an offloading, a support mechanism. But if it's brought in before you've learned the skill, it's the number one way to make sure you will not learn the skill.
Well, my kids are engaged when they scroll tick tock as well. Everyone is engaged with that. But engagement is not synonymous with learning.

By no means can you ever resonate with a screen. You could like it. You could laugh at it. You could love it. Some people will marry it, but you'll never get that empathetic resonance that drives learning because the mechanism simply isn't there.
Neil Postman in 1995 said, no tool has ever been a cure for equity. Tools only exacerbate differences.
Believe it or not, Gen Z is less digitally literate than millennials. Gen Alpha is less digitally literate than Gen X.
As late as 2013, so what, a little over a decade ago, only four of the top 50 universities in the United States allowed kids to use a calculator ever at college. Only four.
Reading is now 54 short sentences with one question about each. To anyone with a half of a brain, that's skimming. That's not reading.
